interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into how food security functioned as a central pillar of geopolitical stabilization and economic rehabilitation in early Cold War East and Southeast Asia. It vividly illustrates the friction between global food distribution mechanisms (the IEFC and FAO) and regional turmoil of the late 1940s, including the Burmese civil war and the collapsing Nationalist position in China. Particularly fascinating is the U.S. Army's proposal for triangular barter trade—leveraging Japanese industrial exports like railroad rolling stock to purchase Siamese rice for ECA transfer to China—demonstrating early occupation strategies to revive Japanese export manufacturing while husbanding scarce dollar reserves. Furthermore, the detailed SCAP agricultural releases from late 1949 highlight how occupation interventions in chemical fertilizer supply, disease control, and modernized statistical crop sampling fostered the rapid recovery of Japan's domestic food supply.
overview: This file (894.61317, covering April 1947 through December 1949) documents the severe food supply challenges facing occupied Japan, international efforts to secure emergency rice imports, and the eventual domestic agricultural recovery under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP). In 1947 and 1948, acute food deficits threatened Japan's economic and political stability, forcing U.S. and occupation authorities to navigate worldwide grain shortages, complex international allocations through the International Emergency Food Council (IEFC), regional unrest in Burma, and innovative triangular barter schemes involving Siamese rice, Japanese manufactured goods, and ECA dollars. By late 1949, the focus shifted to documenting a dramatic resurgence in domestic staple food production, driven by massive fertilizer imports, scientific pest and disease control, improved seed stock, and agrarian cooperation that brought rice yields to their highest levels since 1942.

subfiles.about: Requests background memoranda on Japanese and Korean rice production, distribution, and agrarian policies for an upcoming FAO rice study meeting in Delhi.
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of State Dean Acheson (Department of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State instructs SCAP in Tokyo and USAFIK in Seoul to prepare ten detailed background memoranda on rice in Japan and Korea for presentation at a Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) rice meeting in Delhi. The required topics include production expansion measures, international research cooperation, crop forecasting, handling and storage standards, reserve histories, price structures, land tenure, and nutrition standards. The telegram also urges the declassification of pertinent Natural Resources Section and PCR reports to facilitate the delegation's work at the conference.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to SCAP on FAO Rice Conference Preparations
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), Tokyo

subfiles.about: Transmits extracts from Bangkok concerning the establishment of a Siamese government allocation bureau and shipping committee for rice exports.
subfiles.from: Secretary of State George C. Marshall (Department of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State transmits extracts from Bangkok telegram 570 to the U.S. Embassy in Manila regarding the creation of a new Siamese government Allocation Bureau and Coordinating Shipping Committee to replace the Combined Siamese Rice Commission. Under the new arrangement, export rice will be allocated in accordance with International Emergency Food Council (IEFC) quotas directly to shipping agents under formal contracts. The Embassy is instructed to notify the Philippine Government of these updated administrative procedures.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram to Manila Embassy on Siamese Rice Allocation Machinery

subfiles.about: Urges approval of a 100,000-ton Siamese rice import allocation to alleviate Japan's severe summer staple food ration deficit.
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), Tokyo
subfiles.summary: SCAP strongly advocates requesting 100,000 metric tons of Siamese rice for Japanese civilian consumption, noting that Japan can readily accept grain with a high proportion of broken or glutinous rice. The telegram emphasizes that arriving during the critical summer period, when the rice component of the staple ration falls to a low of three days per month, the shipment will provide economic and social stability far out of proportion to the quantity involved. It also confirms vessel fixtures coordinated with the American Embassy in Bangkok to lift initial and prospective cargoes.
subfiles.title: SCAP Telegram on Urgent Need for Siamese Rice Imports
subfiles.to: Department of the Army and Department of State

subfiles.about: Reports that Burmese rice exports are severely curtailed by insurgent unrest and cannot be spared for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The U.S. Military Attaché in Rangoon informs SCAP that despite Burma dispatching a three-man trade delegation to Tokyo, it is hopeless for Japan to expect any Burmese rice imports. Insurgent activity in Lower Burma since August has drastically curtailed rice exports, leaving Burma struggling to fulfill existing IEFC allocations to India, Ceylon, Malaya, and China. The Embassy advises that proposing rice allocations for Japan to the Burmese government would be futile and urges strict adherence to established IEFC procedures.
subfiles.title: Rangoon Military Attaché Telegram on Impossibility of Burmese Rice Shipments to Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP), Tokyo

subfiles.about: Records inter-agency discussions on allocating rice to Japan through the IEFC and an Army proposal for triangular trade involving Siam, Japan, and China.
subfiles.from: W. S. McCornick (Division of Commercial Policy, Department of State)
subfiles.summary: State Department, Army, and Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) representatives met to discuss upcoming IEFC rice allocations for Japan using GARIOA funds. Army officials introduced an innovative triangular trade scheme under which Japan's Board of Trade (Boeki Cho) would barter manufactured goods, such as railroad equipment, for Siamese rice and resell the rice to ECA for dollars to meet aid commitments to China. ECA officials showed interest but noted potential political objections from Nationalist China and statutory constraints if U.S. domestic rice were declared surplus.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum of Conversation on IEFC Rice Allocation and Triangular Trade

subfiles.about: Transmits a GHQ Far East Command press release estimating the 1949 Japanese rice harvest at 9,832,000 metric tons.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald (U.S. Political Adviser to SCAP, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: USPOLAD Tokyo transmits an official GHQ press release reporting the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry's preliminary estimate of the 1949 rice crop at 9,832,000 metric tons, reviewed by SCAP's Natural Resources Section. Although late-season typhoons, rice blast, and pests caused severe regional damage in Kyushu, Tohoku, and Kinki, the yield was 5 percent above the 1931-1940 prewar average and the highest since 1942. The report details statistical sampling methods, planted acreage, and harvested areas compared with 1948.
subfiles.title: USPOLAD Tokyo Airgram Transmitting 1949 Japanese Rice Crop Estimate

subfiles.about: Transmits a GHQ SCAP press release documenting postwar recovery in Japan's staple food production up to 1949.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald (U.S. Political Adviser to SCAP, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: USPOLAD Tokyo forwards a GHQ SCAP press release detailing the remarkable rebound of Japanese agriculture from the disastrous 1945 postwar low of 9.9 million metric tons to 14.4 million metric tons brown rice equivalents in 1949. The release attributes this recovery to substantial increases in domestic and imported chemical fertilizers, improved seed varieties, insect and disease control, and the industrious labor of Japanese farmers. It emphasizes the need for ongoing government-farmer cooperation, equitable quota allocations, depoliticized crop reporting, and sound economic incentives.
subfiles.title: USPOLAD Tokyo Airgram on Postwar Japanese Staple Food Production Recovery
